title: Percentage and Its Applications
summary: Percent means 'per hundred': 64% = 64/100 = 0.64. To change a percent to a fraction or decimal, drop % and divide by 100 (0.2% = 0.002); to change a fraction or decimal to a percent, multiply by 100 (16/25 = 64%, 3.7 = 370%, 0.025 = 2.5%). x% of a quantity = (x/100) × quantity. To find what percent A is of B, work out (A/B) × 100. Percentage increase or decrease = (change ÷ original value) × 100 — a fall from 150 to 100 is 50/150 × 100 = 33⅓%.
Successive changes multiply: +20% then −20% gives 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, a net 4% decrease. If a price falls by r%, a fixed sum buys more; work with the money saved.

Cost price (C.P.) is what is paid, including overheads such as repairs and transport; selling price (S.P.) is what the article is sold for. Profit = S.P. − C.P.; loss = C.P. − S.P. Profit% = profit/C.P. × 100 and loss% = loss/C.P. × 100 — always on the C.P. S.P. = C.P. × (100 + gain%)/100 and S.P. = C.P. × (100 − loss%)/100. If C.P. = S.P. there is no profit and no loss.

Discount is a reduction on the marked (list) price: S.P. = M.P. − discount, and discount% = discount/M.P. × 100. A shopkeeper who marks goods 20% above cost and allows 10% discount sells at 1.2 × 0.9 = 1.08 of cost — a gain of 8%. Successive discounts are applied one after another, not added.
S.I. = P × R × T / 100, where P is the principal, R the rate per annum and T the time in years (6 months = ½ year). Amount = P + S.I. A sum doubles when S.I. = P, i.e. R × T = 100.

A = P(1 + R/100)ⁿ, C.I. = A − P. When interest is compounded half-yearly, use R/2 per half-year and 2n periods: ₹12,000 at 4% for 1½ years half-yearly gives A = 12000 × (1.02)³ = ₹12,734.50. C.I. equals S.I. for the first period and is larger after that.

A value that grows at r% a year becomes V₀(1 + r/100)ⁿ; one that depreciates becomes V₀(1 − r/100)ⁿ. If the rate changes each year, multiply the year factors: a car worth ₹5,50,000 losing 15% in the first year and 10% in each later year is worth 550000 × 0.85 × 0.9 × 0.9 = ₹3,78,675 after 3 years. Population growth, business profit and loss, and machine depreciation are all worked this way.

mcq: When 60 is reduced to 45, the reduction percent is —
the principal remains the same every year
the interest is the same for each year

mcq.work: In compound interest the interest of each year is added to the principal, so the principal for the next year is larger — it changes every year.

mcq: The cost price of 10 articles equals the selling price of 8 articles. The gain or loss percent is —

mcq.work:
Let C.P. of one article = ₹1; then C.P. of 10 = ₹10 = S.P. of 8, so S.P. of one = 10/8 = ₹1.25.
Gain = 0.25 on 1 ⇒ 25% gain.

vsa: By reducing the selling price of an article by ₹50, a 5% gain turns into a 5% loss. Find the original selling price.

The change from +5% to −5% is 10% of the C.P.
10% of C.P. = 50 ⇒ C.P. = ₹500.
Original S.P. = 500 × 105/100 = ₹525.

The cost price of 25 articles equals the selling price of 20. Find the gain percent.

Let C.P. of one article = ₹1. C.P. of 25 = ₹25 = S.P. of 20, so S.P. of one = 25/20 = ₹1.25.
Gain = 0.25 on 1 ⇒ 25%.

vsa: A 10% fall in the price of tea lets a man buy 25 kg more for ₹20,000. Find the original and reduced prices per kg.

10% of 20000 = ₹2,000 is saved, and it buys the extra 25 kg.
Reduced price = 2000/25 = ₹80 per kg.
Original price = 80 × 100/90 = ₹88.89 per kg.

In an election 75% of the voters cast their votes. The winner got 51% of the votes cast, which was 1530 votes. Find the total number of voters.

Let there be V voters. Votes cast = 0.75V; winner's votes = 0.51 × 0.75V = 0.3825V.
0.3825V = 1530 ⇒ V = 4000.
A shopkeeper sells rice at a profit of 10% and uses a weight which is 10% less than the actual weight. Find his total gain.

For each 1 kg he charges for, he gives only 900 g.
Let the cost of 1 kg be ₹100: his cost is ₹90 (for 900 g) and he charges ₹110 (10% profit on 1 kg).
Gain = 110 − 90 = ₹20 on ₹90 ⇒ 20/90 × 100 = 22.22%.
